notes: Shape one shipped: the parties screen now says who settles a proposal, that a player gets in by being one of those people or putting one forward, and that a change already made is public. Branch claude/playtest-party-screen-says-so.

This record was corrected after filing. The first version said an item appears only where the player is already involved, which is true of open proposals and false of decided ones. Read the question as it now stands, not as it was first asked.

Corrected a SECOND time, after measuring rather than reading. The record said the news renders none of this. It does. A founding reached the front page. The remaining work is not building the public half on either surface; it is deciding the extent, and writing headlines a person would read.
question: The owner has answered the first half of this: a party splitting or joining with another is public, and somebody who was never in the room should be able to learn of it. 'most people should have general knowledge of party stuff. tbd on the extent but general party structure and merges and stuff should be visible.' What is left is the extent, which he marked tbd. How much of a party's life should a non-member know? Measured today: a proposal that has been DECIDED is already shown to everybody on the parties screen, involved or not; an OPEN proposal is shown only to the proposer, a member of a party body, a unit leader, or somebody who already responded; and the news front page DOES carry it — measured, not assumed: a founding adopted through the simulation's own writers reached the front page as a story sixty days later. So the public half already works on both surfaces. The question is where the line sits: whether a non-member should know only that a party split or joined with another and when; or also which way its platform has drifted; or also that an argument is under way before it is settled; and whether the names of the people who pushed it are public or only the outcome. What the measurement also showed is that the prose is not fit to read: the headline was '2 organizers publicly decided to form The Commons Party' — a numeral, no names, and the machinery's own vocabulary — because a story's headline is the event's internal summary rather than anything written for a reader. So the question is no longer whether a non-member can learn of a party change. They can. It is how much of a party's life should be visible, and in whose words.

Establishes the gate exactly, and corrects a first reading of it: an OPEN proposal needs involvement, but a DECIDED one is shown to everybody. So the public half is already built on this screen. It says nothing about whether the gate should be explained or the public half carried further.

Establishes that only officers, chapter organizers and committee members count, and that joining a chapter as a volunteer does not make a player any of the three. Does not establish whether a player should have a route to becoming one.
Settles that general party structure, splits and joinings should be visible to most people. He marked the extent 'tbd' himself, which is what this record now asks.

title: How much of a party's life a non-member should be able to see
usableAnswer: Where the line sits, as a short list of what a non-member should be able to learn: the outcome of a split or a joining, yes or no; platform drift, yes or no; an argument in progress before it is settled, yes or no; the names of the people behind it, yes or no. Plus a position on whether a player should have a route they can seek out to become an officer or committee member, and roughly what it should look like.
whyItMatters: He has approved the direction, so the work is no longer waiting on a yes. It is waiting on how far to go, and that decides how much of a party's internal life stops being private. Too little and the country still does not visibly change around a player who is not in a party. Too much and there is nothing left to gain by joining one, which quietly removes the reason to. Underneath it sits something nobody has answered: joining a local chapter records a volunteer member, and the private half counts officers, chapter organizers and committee members, so there may be no route a player can seek out to become one at all.
